title: The Polyhedral Stretching Theorem
theorem: Stretch any solid with equal edges one edge-length in any direction and every edge stays the same length: the Platonic solids, DICTO's stretched dodecahedra, three and four caps, and paper models to build them
inshort: Take a regular dodecahedron and slide it one edge-length in a straight line. The shape it sweeps through has every edge the same length, whichever way you slide it, except when the slide runs exactly along one of its edges. Its faces are the dodecahedron's twelve pentagons and a belt of rhombi, ten or twelve of them; where the slide lies flat along a pentagon, that pentagon stretches into a hexagon or a heptagon. Sliding along a cube axis gives DICTO's stretched dodecahedron (F11); along a five-fold axis the ten rhombi are all alike; sliding along a face diagonal of Euclid's cube gives the member DICTO found, all twelve pentagons and ten rhombi, which began as a void and two overlapping dodecahedra that DICTO saw in the dodecahedron layer of paper #47. Placing dodecahedra at the corners of a triangle or a tetrahedron gives the three- and four-cap forms, with equilateral triangles among their faces. The same theorem holds for every solid whose edges are all equal, so for every Platonic solid; the stretched icosahedra form a second new-looking family, and the tetrahedron and octahedron rediscover the cuboctahedron, the truncated tetrahedron and three Johnson solids. title: One Move Each: Classical Cut-and-Glue Space-Fillers Built Exactly
theorem: Theorem: the regular-hexagon elongated dodecahedron, the Bain rhombic dodecahedron, the elongated dodecahedron as a type, the Bilinski dodecahedron and the 60° rhombohedron, known from cutting, gluing, zone removal or drawings, each come from one setting of Kaleidohedra's lattice moves, with exact corners, volumes and symmetry
inshort: Books describe several classical solids that fill space by how to make them from other solids: shave a belt off one, stick two pyramids onto another, glue a few slanted bricks together. Kaleidohedra makes the same solids in one go, by tilting and stretching a lattice of points, and so gives every corner and every volume exactly. The moves themselves are Fedorov's (1885); what this paper adds is the exact data, the settings and the proofs. Main theorem. Five space-fillers that the literature gives by cutting, gluing, zone removal or a drawing are each obtained exactly by one setting of Kaleidohedra's three moves: a shear of the lattice, the equal-edged cell (Cell = 1) and a stretch along a free direction. title: The Golden Split: Icosahedra, Unborns and AXE Become Two Convex Space-Fillers

inshort: Icosahedra cannot fill space on their own. Set them in a cubic grid, edge to edge, and two kinds of gap are left: a squeezed icosahedron (the Unborn) in the middle of each cube, and thin tetrahedra (the AXE) in the faces between them, six per cube. The AXE is the awkward one: wherever it is glued, it sticks out. We cut each AXE into four little pyramids from one inner point and hand each pyramid to the piece it touches. At exactly one point, 1/φ of the way along the AXE's axis, the golden point, nothing sticks out any more: the icosahedra and the Unborns both become truncated octahedra, relatives of Kelvin's foam cell, and these two fill space with no gap. title: The Delian Bond: Samson, Delilah and the Octet Between Kepler's Rhombic Dodecahedron and the Cube
theorem: Theorem: one flat cut, slid through every tetrahedron–octahedron pair of the octet, gives a family of pairs of convex solids that fill space, from Kepler's rhombic dodecahedron through the octet to the cube; at one cut the two solids, DICTO's Samson and Delilah, have exactly equal volume, twice the octet's tetrahedron and half its octahedron, and two other cuts make every edge equal
inshort: Regular tetrahedra and octahedra fill space together: the octet. Join each tetrahedron's centre to each octahedron's centre through the face they share, and the octet falls into double cones, one per shared face. Cut every double cone by one flat plane parallel to that face, and give each side to its own centre. Slide the cut, and the tetrahedra grow while the octahedra shrink, or the other way: every position still fills space with two convex solids. At one end are Kepler's rhombic dodecahedra, a third of the way along the octet, at the other end cubes. At one position the two solids have exactly the same volume: the tetrahedron's has doubled and the octahedron's halved, the doubling of the ancient Delian problem, in both directions at once. DICTO named this pair Samson and Delilah. Main theorem. For every cut position t from 0 to 1 the two pieces are convex and fill space face to face; for t ≤ 1/3 they are a regular tetrahedron of edge 3t and a rhombic dodecahedron with its eight three-fold corners cut, for t ≥ 1/3 a regular octahedron of edge a = 3(1 − t)/2 and a cube with four alternate corners cut, with exact volumes. title: David and Goliath: Jessen's Icosahedron and the Tetrahedron in the A15 Weight Walk
theorem: Theorem: in the A15 (Cr 3 Si) structure, the power diagram with weight difference 3/4 between the Si and Cr sites is exactly a face-to-face tiling of space by Goliath, the convex hull of Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron, and David, a tetragonal disphenoid, two Goliaths and six Davids per cubic cell.
inshort: Paper #53 [1] slid one number, a weight, between the two kinds of points of ten crystal arrangements and recorded, exactly, every tiling of space that appears on the way. In the A15 alloy structure (the arrangement of Cr 3 Si, and of the Weaire–Phelan foam) one stop stood out: at weight difference 3/4 the space-filling pieces are a 20-faced icosahedron around every Si point and a small tetrahedron around every Cr point. DICTO named the pair Goliath and David. Here we prove the stop exactly and identify Goliath: its corners are exactly those of Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron, so Goliath is that famous non-convex solid's convex hull. Goliath has the same shape as the classical Z12 icosahedron of A15 (Frank and Kasper), and the whole tiling is the classical picture of A15 as icosahedra and tetrahedral holes, moved by half a body diagonal; that picture is known. What we did not find in the sources searched is that the weight walk lands exactly on it, at 3/4, and the plain statement that the A15 icosahedron is Jessen's convex hull. title: One Turn Is a Gnomon: the Golden Cycle Step by Step, and the Polar of the Keyed Pair
theorem: Theorem: in DICTO's twelve-station golden cycle, one whole turn is a gnomon in the classical sense of Euclid and Heron, and no shorter run of steps is; within the turn from I, its last step is the only step whose new whole is similar to an earlier station. The keyed DICTONIC pair is the golden pair with eight Tricaps moved from one piece to the other (the Icosaxes minus eight, the Unborn Axes plus the same eight), and the golden pair's polars are cubes with face pyramids of heights 1/φ and 1/φ², which add up to Kepler's rhombic dodecahedron
inshort: Take a square of 3 × 3 dots and add an L-shaped strip of 3 + 4 dots along two sides: you get the next square, 4 × 4. The strip is a gnomon: in the classical definition (Euclid, and Heron in general), the piece which, added to a figure, makes a whole of the same shape as the figure, only larger. The gnomon method as reported for Júlia Pimentel works with exactly this strip, n + (n + 1). DICTO's idea was to carry that structure into three dimensions: walk through his golden cycle of twelve nested solids, from an icosahedron out to the next icosahedron φ³ times larger, and check at every step what it adds and whether the new whole has the shape of something before it. We built every step exactly. The answer is clean. The whole turn is a classical gnomon: the next icosahedron has the same shape as the first. No single step and no shorter run of steps is: no station has the shape of any other station, except the two icosahedra. So it is the last step, from M to the next icosahedron, that closes the gnomon. Step by step, the cycle adds spikes, pyramids, Shields and other pieces that never repeat their shapes. inshort: This paper is about webs of bonds: when pieces fill space, each shared face is a bond, and the bonds together make a network that rewires as the pieces change (#52, #53 [6, 1]). Here we follow that network on a second stacking, and show that keys change the pieces but never the network. Stack them in the hexagonal way (ABAB…), each layer a mirror image of its neighbours across it, and the gaps are the same octahedra and tetrahedra, joined across the mirror planes: the twinned octet. Paper #53 [1] slid one number, a weight, between the two kinds of gap and recorded every way space splits on the way. We follow the same walk on the twinned octet. title: The Global Web of Bonds: How Bonds Hand Over Across Crystal Networks
theorem: Theorem: for ten classical two-kind crystal site sets, and one three-kind set, the weighted Voronoi (power) diagram is computed exactly along the whole weight line on which both kinds have cells: every flip, the bonds on every interval, and every point where only unlike bonds exist. The two hand-overs of the DICTONIC loops, gradual and with a single switch, both recur.
inshort: Paper #52 [3] showed that DICTO's two loops of space-filling pairs are one fixed crowd of points of two kinds, with one number, a weight, slid between the kinds; the bonds (one line for each face two pieces share) form a web. In the golden loop the two like bonds hand over gradually; in the Delian loop they hand over all at once, at the octet, where only bonds between unlike pieces are left. DICTO proposed that these branches turn up elsewhere in slightly different guises. We took eight more crystal arrangements of two kinds of points (three in the plane, five in space) and one of three kinds, and slid the weight through every value at which both kinds still have a piece. For each we found, exactly, every point where the pattern changes, which bonds exist in between, and whether there is a moment with only unlike bonds. The proposal holds: the hand-over with a single switch recurs in the square lattice with its centres, in the honeycomb with its hexagon centres (the switch is the trihexagonal tiling) and in rock salt; the gradual hand-over recurs in zinc blende, in the holes of hexagonal close packing, and in the A15 and C15 alloy structures. title: The Web of Bonds: How the DICTONIC Bonds Hand Over
theorem: Theorem: both DICTONIC loops are weighted Voronoi (power) diagrams of one fixed crowd of points of two kinds, with one weight slid between the kinds; the bonds are the edges of the dual weighted-Delaunay web; the bond between unlike pieces never breaks inside a loop, while the two like bonds hand over, gradually in the golden loop and all at once, at the octet, in the Delian loop
inshort: DICTO's two loops of space-filling pairs, the golden loop of paper #48 and the Delian loop of paper #51, each slide one pair of solids through a whole family of shapes. Draw one line, a bond, between every two pieces that share a face, and the lines make a web. We show that each loop is really one fixed crowd of points of two kinds, the piece centres, and that the only thing that moves is one number, a weight given to one kind against the other. Every piece is the region nearer (in this weighted sense) to its own point than to any other. Then the web is exactly the web of the classical weighted Delaunay construction. As the weight slides, the bond between unlike pieces never breaks. title: The Rule of Halves: the Holes of Every Close-Packed Stacking
theorem: Theorem: in every close-packed stacking, along the whole weight walk, each tetrahedral hole's piece is the piece of the cubic or the hexagonal stacking named by its nearest layer, and each octahedral hole's piece is a top half and a bottom half, each the half of the cubic or the hexagonal piece named by the layer on that side; so the pieces of all stackings are finite in kind and an octahedral piece's volume is always the mean of its two parents' volumes.
inshort: Stack layers of balls and the gaps between them are small octahedra and tetrahedra. Stack them in the cubic way (ABCABC…) or the hexagonal way (ABAB…) and these gaps are arranged differently; crystals also use countless mixed stackings, such as ABAC or ABCACB. In papers #51, #53 and #56 we slid one number, a weight, between the two kinds of gap and followed how space is shared out among them: the web of bonds. Here we follow it on every stacking at once, and find a simple rule. A tetrahedral gap always takes the piece it would have in the pure stacking of the layer it sits closest to. An octahedral gap sits half-way between two layers, and its piece is two halves: the top half is the top half of the cubic or the hexagonal piece, as the layer above decides, and the bottom half likewise from the layer below. So every stacking, of any length or pattern, is built from the two pure ones, and the kinds of piece are finite: we list them all, with exact volumes.
